children.title: Exactness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Primitive, formulation, and partition regimes in which lower bounding loses no objective information.

children.title: Primitive Envelope Exactness
children.top_down_role: Exact convexification of individual nonlinear primitives.

knowledge_statements.title: Primitive Envelope Exactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact convex-hull representation for one nonlinear primitive over a bounded domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, and let \(\phi:D\to\mathbb R\) be continuous. Its convex envelope is \[(\operatorname{vex}_D\phi)(x)=\sup\{g(x):g\text{ is convex on }D,\ g\le\phi\text{ on }D\}.\] The primitive epigraph relaxation \(t\ge(\operatorname{vex}_D\phi)(x)\) is exact in the convexification sense: \[\operatorname{epi}_D(\operatorname{vex}_D\phi)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}_D\phi).\] Thus using the convex envelope introduces no loss beyond taking the closed convex hull of that primitive's epigraph; it need not convexify interactions with other constraints exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primitive convex envelope represents exactly the closed convex hull of that primitive’s restricted epigraph, but not necessarily the joint model.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}_D(\operatorname{vex}_D\phi)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}_D\phi)\).

notation.meaning: convex envelope of the primitive on D

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

children.title: Joint Formulation Exactness
children.top_down_role: Exactness obtained only after joint or lifted convexification.

assumptions_latex: \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^p\times\mathbb{R}\) is a closed convex lifted relaxation satisfying \(\operatorname{epi}_X f\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_{x,t}Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_{x,t}Q=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}_X f)\), and hence \(\min_{(x,y,t)\in Q}t=\min_{x\in X}f(x)\).

notation.meaning: Projection onto the original variable and epigraph coordinate.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness is defined through the projected lifted epigraph, not through separate envelopes of primitive expressions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A lifted convex formulation \(Q\) is jointly exact for minimizing \(f\) on \(X\) when its projection onto the original variable and epigraph coordinate satisfies \[\operatorname{proj}_{x,t}Q=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}_X f).\] Consequently, optimizing the lifted relaxation gives \[\min_{(x,y,t)\in Q}t=\min_{x\in X}f(x).\] Exactness concerns the complete joint formulation; individual relaxed primitives need not equal their separate convex envelopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lifted relaxation is jointly exact when its projected epigraph is the closed convex hull of the original epigraph, so its lower bound equals the global minimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Joint Formulation Exactness

children.title: Finite-Refinement Exactness
children.top_down_role: Exact lower bounds after finitely many partitions, cuts, or disaggregations.

assumptions_latex: \(R_0\supseteq R_1\supseteq\cdots\) are valid convex relaxations produced by successive refinements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite-refinement exactness holds precisely when \(\min_{(x,t)\in R_K}t=\min_{x\in X}f(x)\) for some finite \(K\).

notation.meaning: Number of refinements required for exactness.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is finite exactness of the optimal lower bound, weaker than exact recovery of the entire convexified epigraph.

source_refs.locator: 3.6 Finite epsilon-Convergence and epsilon-Global Optimality p. 87

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f^*=\min_{x\in X}f(x)\), and define the relaxation bound \(L_k=\min\{t:(x,t)\in R_k\}\). The refinement scheme has finite-refinement exactness on this instance if there is a finite index \(K\) such that \[L_K=f^*.\] Validity and nesting imply \(L_k\leq L_{k+1}\leq f^*\); therefore equality persists for every \(k\geq K\). The refinements may be partitions, valid cuts, liftings, or disaggregations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-refinement exactness means that after finitely many valid refinements, the relaxation lower bound equals the true global optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Refinement Exactness

source_witnesses.locator: 3.6 Finite epsilon-Convergence and epsilon-Global Optimality p. 87

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition itself is intelligible, but the principal locator concerns finite epsilon-convergence, which does not establish attainment of exact equality after finitely many refinements. A source specifically supporting finite exact lower-bound attainment, or a clearly identified class of refinements for which it holds, is required.

children.title: Cost–Strength Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Construction, representation, and solution costs associated with stronger lower models.

children.title: Bound Generation-Validation Cost
children.top_down_role: Cost of generating coefficients, enclosures, cuts, and validity certificates.

children.title: Construction Cost
children.top_down_role: Computational burden of generating relaxation coefficients, enclosures, or cuts.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\mathrm{gen}}(D;\mathcal{B},M)\) is the total resource usage before the bound representation is available.

notation.meaning: Construction cost under computation model M.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction excludes subsequent validation and optimization of the generated relaxation.

source_refs.locator: 3.5.2 Model Variants and Solution Approaches p. 193

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The construction cost of a convex lower bound is \(C_{\mathrm{gen}}(D;\mathcal{B},M)\), the resources consumed by \(\mathcal{B}\) on encoded instance \(D\) under model \(M\) to produce an explicit or oracle-accessible bound representation. The resource vector may count arithmetic operations, oracle calls, elapsed time, and working memory. It includes partitioning, coefficient generation, lifting, and cut generation, but excludes independent validation and solution of the resulting relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Construction cost measures the computation and memory needed to generate a usable convex lower-bound representation, before validation or relaxation solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Construction Cost

source_witnesses.locator: 3.5.2 Model Variants and Solution Approaches p. 193

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Construction Cost, but the cited stochastic-model section does not inspectably support the proposed resource vector or the boundary between construction, validation, and solution costs. A complexity or formulation-generation source is needed.

children.title: Certification Cost
children.top_down_role: Computational burden of establishing validity for generated lower models.

assumptions_latex: \(g\) is a proposed lower bound on domain \(X\).
\(V\) is a specified validation procedure and computation model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\mathrm{cert}}(D,g;V)\) counts the resources required to establish \(g(x)\leq f(x)\) for every \(x\in X\) and any claimed convexity of \(g\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certification concerns validity of a generated bound, not the cost of finding or optimizing it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The certification cost \(C_{\mathrm{cert}}(D,g;V)\) is the resource usage of procedure \(V\) required to verify that \(g\) is a valid lower bound, namely \[g(x)\leq f(x)\quad\text{for every }x\in X,\] together with convexity of \(g\) when convexity is claimed. Resources may include arithmetic operations, symbolic checks, oracle calls, proof-object size, and memory. A construction with no independently checkable certificate may have low generation cost but high certification cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Certification cost measures the work needed to verify that a proposed function is convex when claimed and never exceeds the original objective on its domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Certification Cost

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Certification Cost and is internally coherent, but the cited convex-lower-bounding section does not inspectably support this computational certification-cost model, including proof-object size and independent validation effort.

children.title: Generation–Validation Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Cost balance between model generation plus validity assessment.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal{B}_1\) and \(\mathcal{B}_2\) generate valid underestimators for the same instance.
\(C_{\mathrm{gen}}\) and \(C_{\mathrm{cert}}\) are measured under common resource models.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Neither method dominates the other when one improves \(L\) or \(C_{\mathrm{gen}}\) but worsens \(C_{\mathrm{cert}}\); admissible choices lie on the Pareto frontier of these criteria.

notation.meaning: Lower bound supplied by underestimator g.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The tradeoff is formalized as Pareto efficiency over strength, generation cost, and validation cost.

source_refs.locator: 3.5.2 Model Variants and Solution Approaches p. 193

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Associate with each construction \(\mathcal{B}\) the criterion vector \[\bigl(-L(g_{\mathcal{B}}),C_{\mathrm{gen}}(\mathcal{B}),C_{\mathrm{cert}}(g_{\mathcal{B}})\bigr),\] where smaller components are preferred. A construction is generation-validation efficient if no alternative weakly decreases all three components and strictly decreases at least one. Thus a bound that is cheap to generate need not be cheap to certify, and additional generation effort is justified only by improved strength or reduced downstream certification cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bound constructions should be compared by Pareto dominance across bound strength, generation cost, and certification cost; improvement in one criterion can worsen another.
knowledge_statements.title: Generation–Validation Tradeoffs

source_witnesses.locator: 3.5.2 Model Variants and Solution Approaches p. 193

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A principle is an appropriate knowledge kind for this terminal container, but the three-criterion Pareto framework is an added formal model not supported by the cited locators. The sources must substantiate the strength-generation-certification comparison and its dominance criterion.

children.title: Model Representation-Solution Cost
children.top_down_role: Size and solver burden of linear, conic, nonlinear, lifted, and nonsmooth models.

children.title: Representation Cost
children.top_down_role: Size of linear, conic, nonlinear, lifted, or nonsmooth relaxation encodings.

assumptions_latex: \(s(R)\) counts scalar representation components under a fixed encoding.
Equivalent formulations are compared using the same encoding conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\mathrm{rep}}(R)=s(R)\), commonly decomposed into counts of variables, constraints, cone dimensions, and nonzero coefficients.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation cost measures model size, independently of the algorithm subsequently used to solve it.

source_refs.locator: 3.5.2 Model Variants and Solution Approaches p. 193

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed encoding, the representation cost of relaxation \(R\) is \[C_{\mathrm{rep}}(R)=s(R).\] The size functional \(s\) records the scalar data required to store or transmit \(R\), such as numbers of original and auxiliary variables, equality and inequality constraints, aggregate cone dimension, and nonzero coefficients. Representation costs are comparable only after fixing coefficient encoding and whether structured operators are stored implicitly or expanded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Representation cost is the encoded size of a relaxation, including variables, constraints, cone dimensions, coefficients, and any auxiliary structure made explicit.
knowledge_statements.title: Representation Cost

source_witnesses.locator: 3.5.2 Model Variants and Solution Approaches p. 193

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is suitable for Representation Cost, but the equality \(C_{\mathrm{rep}}(R)=s(R)\) and the stated encoding conventions are not supported by the cited representation and model-variant locators as currently inspectable.

children.title: Solution Cost
children.top_down_role: Solver effort associated with the chosen convex representation.

assumptions_latex: \(R\) is a convex relaxation with encoded input length \(s(R)\).
\(A\) is a specified solver using a fixed oracle and arithmetic model.
\(\varepsilon>0\) is the requested objective or feasibility accuracy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\mathrm{sol}}(R,A,\varepsilon)\) is the resource usage required by \(A\) to return an \(\varepsilon\)-accurate solution or a declared certificate of failure.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solution cost is conditional on the formulation, solver, oracle model, and requested numerical accuracy.

source_refs.locator: 3.5.2 Model Variants and Solution Approaches p. 193

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The solution cost \(C_{\mathrm{sol}}(R,A,\varepsilon)\) is the time, arithmetic operations, oracle calls, and memory used by algorithm \(A\) to solve convex relaxation \(R\) to tolerance \(\varepsilon\). The accuracy convention must specify objective error, feasibility residual, or a primal-dual gap. Because equivalent convex sets can have different encodings, \(C_{\mathrm{sol}}\) depends on both the represented set and its formulation, not solely on representation size \(s(R)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solution cost measures resources used to solve a particular relaxation formulation to a stated accuracy under a specified solver and computational model.
knowledge_statements.title: Solution Cost

source_witnesses.locator: 3.5.2 Model Variants and Solution Approaches p. 193

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and scope match Solution Cost, but the cited model-variants section does not inspectably support the solver-, oracle-, tolerance-, and failure-certificate definition. A convex-optimization complexity source with a precise computational model is required.

children.title: Lifted-Model Burden
children.top_down_role: Auxiliary-variable plus constraint overhead in extended representations.

assumptions_latex: \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+p}\) is a lifted formulation with \(\operatorname{proj}_x Q=R\).
Both formulations use fixed scalar encodings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lift adds \(p\) auxiliary variables and the additional encoded constraints and coefficients of \(Q\), even when its projection is stronger or simpler.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The burden records explicit auxiliary structure; it does not imply that lifted formulations are computationally inferior.

source_refs.locator: 3.5.2 Model Variants and Solution Approaches p. 193

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+p}\) satisfies \(\operatorname{proj}_xQ=R\), its lifted-model burden relative to an original-space formulation of \(R\) includes \(p\) auxiliary variables and every additional encoded constraint, coefficient, and cone block used to describe \(Q\). This burden may increase storage and per-iteration linear-algebra cost. It is not an ordering of total solution cost: lifting may simultaneously yield a tighter relaxation or a more tractable conic representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lifted model adds auxiliary variables and representation data, although the added size may be offset by stronger bounds or a more tractable formulation.
knowledge_statements.title: Lifted-Model Burden

source_witnesses.locator: 3.5.2 Model Variants and Solution Approaches p. 193

children.title: Refinement Efficiency
children.top_down_role: Bound improvement obtained from partitions, cuts, liftings, or disaggregation.

assumptions_latex: \(R\) is a valid relaxation with lower bound \(L(R)\).
\(\rho\) is a refinement producing a valid relaxation \(R^\rho\subseteq R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\eta(\rho\mid R)=\bigl(L(R^\rho)-L(R)\bigr)/C(\rho)\geq0\) measures lower-bound improvement per unit incremental cost.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Efficiency is marginal and depends on the chosen cost normalization and current relaxation.

source_refs.locator: 3.5.2 Model Variants and Solution Approaches p. 193

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimization, let \(L(R)\) denote the optimal value of relaxation \(R\). If refinement \(\rho\) gives \(R^\rho\subseteq R\) at incremental cost \(C(\rho)>0\), its marginal efficiency is \[\eta(\rho\mid R)=\frac{L(R^\rho)-L(R)}{C(\rho)}.\] Validity and inclusion imply \(\eta(\rho\mid R)\geq0\). Comparisons require the same cost units and bound normalization; partitions, cuts, liftings, and disaggregations can then be ranked by realized improvement per unit cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Refinement efficiency is the increase in a valid minimization lower bound divided by the incremental cost of the partition, cut, lifting, or disaggregation.
knowledge_statements.title: Refinement Efficiency

source_witnesses.locator: 3.5.2 Model Variants and Solution Approaches p. 193

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition matches Refinement Efficiency and is mathematically coherent, but the specific marginal ratio and normalization requirements are not inspectably supported by either cited locator. A source defining or analyzing bound improvement per unit refinement cost is required.

children.title: Structural Complexity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Scaling differences across dense, separable, decomposable, and sparse interaction structures.

children.title: Dimensional Scaling
children.top_down_role: Growth of relaxation size or computational burden with ambient dimension.

assumptions_latex: Coordinate \(i\) is divided into \(m_i\geq1\) nonempty intervals.
The encoded construction stores at least one scalar component for every resulting box.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The number of boxes is \(N=\prod_{i=1}^d m_i\), and the representation size \(S\) satisfies \(S=\Omega(N)\); if \(m_i=m>1\), then \(N=m^d\).

notation.meaning: Scalar representation size of the partition-based construction.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The bound concerns full Cartesian partitioning; adaptive or sparse refinements can use fewer cells.

source_refs.locator: 3.6 Finite epsilon-Convergence and epsilon-Global Optimality p. 87

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Independent coordinate partitioning of \(X=\prod_{i=1}^d[a_i,b_i]\), with \(m_i\) intervals on coordinate \(i\), produces exactly \[N=\prod_{i=1}^d m_i\] Cartesian boxes. If the construction stores at least one scalar component per box, its representation size \(S\) satisfies \[S=\Omega(N).\] Under uniform refinement \(m_i=m>1\), the cell count becomes \(N=m^d\), exhibiting exponential dimensional scaling for the full tensor partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Cartesian partition with \(m_i\) intervals per coordinate has \(N=\prod_i m_i\) cells. Any encoding storing at least one scalar component per cell has size \(\Omega(N)\), and uniform \(m\)-way refinement creates \(m^d\) cells in dimension \(d\).
knowledge_statements.title: Dimensional Scaling

source_witnesses.locator: 3.6 Finite epsilon-Convergence and epsilon-Global Optimality p. 87

children.title: Structural Decomposability
children.top_down_role: Complexity effects of separable or decomposable interaction patterns.

assumptions_latex: \(X=X_1\times\cdots\times X_q\), with each \(X_j\) nonempty and compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{vex}_X f(x)=\sum_{j=1}^q\operatorname{vex}_{X_j}f_j(x_j)\).

notation.meaning: Convex envelope over the indicated domain.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: This exact decomposition requires disjoint variable blocks and a Cartesian product domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an additively separable function on a Cartesian product, convexification decomposes by blocks: \[\operatorname{vex}_X f(x)=\sum_{j=1}^q\operatorname{vex}_{X_j}f_j(x_j).\] Thus the exact convex underestimator can be constructed from the block envelopes without forming a joint envelope in dimension \(\sum_{j=1}^q\dim X_j\). Coupling constraints or overlapping variable blocks invalidate this identity unless additional consistency conditions are imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a Cartesian product with disjoint additive blocks, the convex envelope of the sum equals the sum of the blockwise convex envelopes.
knowledge_statements.title: Structural Decomposability

children.title: Sparsity Exploitation
children.top_down_role: Complexity reductions available from sparse variable interactions.

assumptions_latex: Each \(g_j\) is convex and satisfies \(g_j(z)\leq f_j(z)\) on the projection \(X_{S_j}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(x)=\sum_{j=1}^q g_j(x_{S_j})\leq f(x)\), and local construction dimensions are at most \(w\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sparsity reduces local construction dimension but does not by itself guarantee that the summed bound is the global convex envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(g(x)=\sum_{j=1}^q g_j(x_{S_j})\). Since every \(g_j\) is convex in its local arguments, \(g\) is convex on \(X\); summing the local inequalities gives \[g(x)\leq\sum_{j=1}^q f_j(x_{S_j})=f(x)\quad\text{for all }x\in X.\] Hence valid underestimation can be assembled from problems of dimension at most \(w=\max_j|S_j|\). Overlapping scopes preserve validity but generally prevent the sum from being the exact convex envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Summing convex underestimators of sparse objective terms gives a valid convex underestimator, with each local construction involving at most the largest scope size.
knowledge_statements.title: Sparsity Exploitation

children.title: Dense-Structure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Scaling behavior when decomposition or sparsity offers limited benefit.

knowledge_statements.title: Dense-Structure Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representational scaling for a family of explicitly encoded, densely coupled convex relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a family of regional convex-relaxation formulations indexed by \(m\), and let \(E_m\subseteq\{\{i,j\}:1\leq i<j\leq m\}\) be the set of explicitly represented pairwise couplings. Suppose there is a constant \(c>0\), independent of \(m\), such that \(|E_m|\geq c\binom{m}{2}\) for all sufficiently large \(m\). If the encoding size \(S_m\) satisfies \(S_m=\Theta(m+|E_m|)\), then \(S_m=\Theta(m^2)\). Thus an explicitly encoded dense coupling model has quadratic representational size; sparsity or bounded-block complexity bounds require additional structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a family of relaxations that explicitly stores a constant fraction of all pairwise couplings, an encoding with constant-size data per coupling has quadratic size in the number of coupled quantities.
assumptions_latex: For each positive integer \(m\), the formulation has \(m\) coupled quantities and an explicitly represented coupling set \(E_m\).
There is a constant \(c>0\), independent of \(m\), such that \(|E_m|\geq c\binom{m}{2}\) for all sufficiently large \(m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The formulation size satisfies \(S_m=\Theta(m^2)\).

notation.meaning: Set of explicitly represented pairwise couplings
Encoding size of the relaxation formulation

children.title: Global-Search Interface
children.top_down_role: Lower-bound services supplied to deterministic partition and branch-and-bound methods.

children.title: Regional Bound Oracles
children.top_down_role: Regional relaxation services attached to search regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Regional Bound Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic lower-bound oracle for minimization over one search region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(f:R\to\mathbb R\) be the objective, let \(g:R\to\mathbb R^q\) define the componentwise constraints, and set \(X_R=\{x\in R:g(x)\leq0\}\) and \(v(R)=\inf_{x\in X_R}f(x)\). A regional bound oracle constructs a convex set \(Q_R\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), a convex function \(\ell_R:Q_R\to\mathbb R\), and a representation map \(\Phi_R:X_R\to Q_R\) satisfying \(\ell_R(\Phi_R(x))\leq f(x)\) for every \(x\in X_R\). It returns \(L(R)=\inf_{z\in Q_R}\ell_R(z)\), together with an optimizer when the infimum is attained or a checkable infeasibility certificate when \(Q_R=\varnothing\). Then \(L(R)\leq v(R)\). The conventions are \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\) and \(L(R)=-\infty\) when the relaxation is unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regional bound oracle solves a valid convex relaxation of a specified search region and returns a certified lower bound, optionally with an attained optimizer or a checkable relaxation-infeasibility certificate.
assumptions_latex: The regional minimization problem has objective \(f:R\to\mathbb R\), constraint map \(g:R\to\mathbb R^q\), and feasible set \(X_R=\{x\in R:g(x)\leq0\}\).

The convex relaxation has feasible set \(Q_R\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), objective \(\ell_R:Q_R\to\mathbb R\), and a map \(\Phi_R:X_R\to Q_R\) such that \(\ell_R(\Phi_R(x))\leq f(x)\) for all \(x\in X_R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle value \(L(R)=\inf_{z\in Q_R}\ell_R(z)\) satisfies \(L(R)\leq v(R)\), and certified emptiness of \(Q_R\) implies \(X_R=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Original feasible set in the region
Map representing original feasible points in the relaxation

children.title: Certified Regional-Elimination Interface
children.top_down_role: Certified regional elimination supported by lower bounds and relaxation infeasibility.

children.title: Fathoming Interface
children.top_down_role: Consumption of regional lower bounds for search-tree elimination.

assumptions_latex: A valid regional lower bound \(L(R)\leq v(R)\) is available.
The incumbent value \(U\) is attained by a globally feasible point, and minimization uses tolerance \(\varepsilon\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(L(R)\geq U-\varepsilon\), then no point in \(R\) can improve the incumbent by more than \(\varepsilon\), so \(R\) may be fathomed.

notation.meaning: Certified lower bound on the regional optimum

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-bound fathoming for deterministic branch-and-bound minimization.

source_refs.locator: 3.12 The GOP in a Branch and Bound Framework p. 114
7.3 Cut and Split (Branch and Bound) Methods p. 176

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization problem, let \(v(R)\) be the optimum restricted to region \(R\), let \(L(R)\leq v(R)\) be a certified relaxation bound, and let \(U\) be the objective value of a feasible incumbent. Given \(\varepsilon\geq0\), the predicate \(L(R)\geq U-\varepsilon\) is a fathoming certificate. Indeed, every feasible \(x\in R\) satisfies \(f(x)\geq v(R)\geq L(R)\geq U-\varepsilon\). The interface may therefore return \((\mathrm{fathom},L(R),U,\varepsilon)\), authorizing removal of \(R\) from the active partition without losing any solution improving \(U\) by more than \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A region is safely fathomed when its certified lower bound cannot improve the feasible incumbent by more than the prescribed tolerance.
knowledge_statements.title: Fathoming Interface

source_witnesses.locator: 3.12 The GOP in a Branch and Bound Framework p. 114

children.title: Exclusion Interface
children.top_down_role: Consumption of validity information for certified regional removal.

assumptions_latex: A predicate \(E_R(x)\) is valid in the sense that every feasible \(x\in R\) satisfies \(E_R(x)\).
A subregion \(S\subseteq R\) is proposed for deletion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If a verifiable certificate establishes \(E_R(x)=\mathrm{false}\) for every \(x\in S\), then \(S\) contains no feasible point and may be excluded.

notation.meaning: Necessary feasibility predicate valid on the parent region

review_flags: interface formulation is broader than any single exclusion operator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility-based exclusion of a subregion, distinct from incumbent-bound fathoming.

source_refs.locator: 7.3 Cut and Split (Branch and Bound) Methods p. 176

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) be a search region and let \(E_R\) be a necessary predicate for original feasibility on \(R\): every \(x\in R\) satisfying the original constraints also satisfies \(E_R(x)\). An exclusion interface accepts a subregion \(S\subseteq R\) and returns an exclusion certificate only when it can verify \(E_R(x)=\mathrm{false}\) for all \(x\in S\). Equivalently, it certifies \(S\cap\{x:E_R(x)\}=\varnothing\). Because the original feasible set in \(S\) is contained in this intersection, deleting \(S\) preserves every feasible point and hence every global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exclusion interface deletes a subregion only after certifying that a necessary feasibility condition fails everywhere on that subregion.
knowledge_statements.title: Exclusion Interface

source_witnesses.locator: 7.3 Cut and Split (Branch and Bound) Methods p. 176

children.title: Relaxation-Infeasibility Signals
children.top_down_role: Infeasibility outcomes used to support regional exclusion.

assumptions_latex: The convex relaxation is an outer relaxation: every originally feasible point in \(R\) has a represented point in \(Q_R\).
The relaxation solver returns a checkable certificate that \(Q_R=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Certified emptiness of \(Q_R\) implies that the original problem has no feasible point in \(R\), so \(R\) may be removed.

notation.meaning: Feasible set of the regional convex relaxation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-way infeasibility implication for valid outer relaxations.

source_refs.locator: 3.12 The GOP in a Branch and Bound Framework p. 114

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_R\) denote the original feasible set in region \(R\), and suppose the relaxation construction maps every \(x\in F_R\) to some \(z\in Q_R\). A relaxation-infeasibility signal is certified only when a solver certificate proves \(Q_R=\varnothing\). Then the inclusion property forces \(F_R=\varnothing\), and the regional problem is infeasible. The converse need not hold: \(Q_R\neq\varnothing\) does not establish original feasibility because the relaxation may contain spurious points. An uncertified numerical status such as failure to find a relaxation point is not an infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Certified infeasibility of a valid outer convex relaxation proves regional infeasibility; relaxation feasibility alone does not prove original feasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation-Infeasibility Signals

source_witnesses.locator: 3.12 The GOP in a Branch and Bound Framework p. 114

children.title: Partition–Quality Feedback
children.top_down_role: Use of relaxation weakness to inform regional refinement.

knowledge_statements.title: Partition–Quality Feedback
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adaptive partition selection driven by a declared, computable relaxation-weakness indicator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input an active partition \(\mathcal P\), certified lower bounds \(L(R)\) for \(R\in\mathcal P\), a feasible incumbent value \(U\), a tolerance \(\varepsilon\geq0\), and declared weakness scores \(\eta(R)\geq0\). If \(L(R)\geq U-\varepsilon\) for every \(R\in\mathcal P\), stop. Otherwise select a region \(R^*\) with \(L(R^*)<U-\varepsilon\) by a declared rule that accounts for bound competitiveness and relaxation weakness, such as lexicographically minimizing \((L(R),-\eta(R))\). Replace \(R^*\) by children \(R_1,\ldots,R_k\) satisfying \(R^*=\bigcup_{j=1}^kR_j\), rebuild their relaxations, and recompute their bounds and weakness scores. Repeat until the stopping test holds or another declared resource limit is reached.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The search repeatedly refines a nonfathomed region selected using both its lower bound and a declared relaxation-weakness score, while child regions preserve coverage of their parent.
assumptions_latex: Each active region \(R\in\mathcal P\) has a certified lower bound \(L(R)\) and a computable, declared weakness score \(\eta(R)\geq0\).
The value \(U\) is attained by a globally feasible point, and \(\varepsilon\geq0\) is an absolute tolerance.
Every split replaces its parent by children whose union equals the parent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every refinement preserves coverage of the active search domain, and the declared score \(\eta(R)\) can prioritize regions diagnosed as having weak relaxations without altering bound validity.

notation.meaning: Certified lower bound for region R

children.title: Polyhedral Outer-Model Refinement Interface
children.top_down_role: Consumption of affine and polyhedral underestimators by successively refined convex models.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Initialization and Conditional Strength of a Polyhedral Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction of a cut-strengthened polyhedral relaxation from a nonlinear convex underestimating relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) denote the polyhedral relaxation \(\min\{c^Tx+c_0:Ax+b\le 0,\ c^Tx+c_0\le \bar v,\ d^Tx_{J_k}\le \bar d\ \forall(d,\bar d)\in N_k,\ k=1,\ldots,p,\ x\in[\underline x,\bar x]\}\), where each \(N_k\) is finite. The relaxation is initialized by constructing an extended reformulation of the nonlinear convex underestimating relaxation \(R\) and then adding cuts. Because \(P\) includes the linearizations of the constraints active at a solution of \(R\), \(\operatorname{val}(P)\ge \operatorname{val}(R)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polyhedral relaxation is initialized from an extended reformulation of the nonlinear convex underestimating relaxation and then augmented with cuts. When it includes the linearizations of the constraints active at a solution of the nonlinear relaxation, its minimum value is at least that of the nonlinear relaxation, so its lower bound is at least as strong.
assumptions_latex: P\text{ includes the linearizations of the constraints active at a solution of }R.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{val}(P)\ge \operatorname{val}(R)

children.title: Underestimator Cut Oracles
children.top_down_role: Interfaces exposing valid affine lower supports.

knowledge_statements.title: Underestimator Cut Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order affine minorant oracle for a finite convex underestimator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a convex set \(C\), a finite convex underestimator \(u:C\to\mathbb R\) of \(f\), and a query point \(\bar x\in C\). Obtain any \(g\in\partial u(\bar x)\) and return the affine cut \(a_{\bar x}(x)=u(\bar x)+g^{\mathsf T}(x-\bar x)\). The subgradient inequality gives \(a_{\bar x}(x)\leq u(x)\leq f(x)\) for all \(x\in C\), while \(a_{\bar x}(\bar x)=u(\bar x)\). If no certified subgradient is available, the oracle returns failure rather than an unvalidated cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a query point, the oracle returns a subgradient affine support that globally underestimates the convex lower model and therefore the original function.
assumptions_latex: A convex underestimator \(u:C\to\mathbb R\) satisfies \(u(x)\leq f(x)\) on a convex set \(C\).
At a query point \(\bar x\in C\), the oracle returns \(g\in\partial u(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The affine function \(a_{\bar x}(x)=u(\bar x)+g^{\mathsf T}(x-\bar x)\) satisfies \(a_{\bar x}(x)\leq u(x)\leq f(x)\) for every \(x\in C\).

notation.meaning: Convex underestimator of the original objective or term
Affine supporting minorant returned at the query point

children.title: Master-Relaxation Management
children.top_down_role: Accumulation and selection of convex lower-model components.

assumptions_latex: Every stored affine component \(a_i\) satisfies \(a_i(x)\leq f(x)\) for all \(x\in C\).
The active index set \(I_k\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The managed master model \(m_k(x)=\max_{i\in I_k}a_i(x)\) is convex and satisfies \(m_k(x)\leq f(x)\) on \(C\); adding valid cuts cannot decrease it.

notation.meaning: Active cut index set at iteration k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-cut management for a piecewise-affine convex master underestimator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a finite active set \(I_0\) of certified affine minorants \(a_i\) on \(C\) and define \(m_k(x)=\max_{i\in I_k}a_i(x)\). Solve the master relaxation using \(m_k\), query for additional valid cuts, and insert selected cuts into \(I_k\). Cuts may be deleted only under a declared retention rule; validity is preserved because every retained \(a_i\leq f\). With insertion only, \(I_k\subseteq I_{k+1}\) implies \(m_k(x)\leq m_{k+1}(x)\leq f(x)\) on \(C\). Stop when the master bound meets the prescribed gap tolerance or no requested cut is returned.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The manager stores selected affine minorants, solves their maximum as a convex master model, and preserves validity under insertion or deletion of valid cuts.
knowledge_statements.title: Master-Relaxation Management

children.title: Domain-Reduction Interface
children.top_down_role: Mutual reinforcement between contracted domains and reconstructed relaxations.

children.title: Range-Tightening Feedback
children.top_down_role: Improved variable and intermediate ranges feeding relaxation reconstruction.

assumptions_latex: The current relaxation is valid for interval bounds \(B\), and bound propagation produces tighter bounds \(B'\subseteq B\).
Every original feasible point consistent with \(B\) also satisfies \(B'\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Reconstructing each range-dependent relaxation component using \(B'\) preserves validity and may strengthen, but must not weaken, the best available regional lower bound when the old model is retained.
review_flags: monotonic strength requires retaining or dominating the prior relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feedback loop from certified tighter ranges to range-dependent relaxation reconstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\) be certified bounds for variables and intermediate expressions, and let \(B'\subseteq B\) be tighter bounds containing every originally feasible realization. Recompute each envelope, secant, or other range-dependent convex relaxation component on \(B'\). The reconstructed model remains an outer relaxation because no feasible realization was removed. To guarantee nondecreasing strength, combine the new model with the retained old model, or verify that the new feasible set is contained in the old one. Under minimization this gives \(L(B')\geq L(B)\), where \(L(B)\) denotes the resulting certified lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Certified tighter ranges are fed back into range-dependent envelopes; retaining the old model guarantees that reconstruction cannot reduce the lower bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Range-Tightening Feedback

children.title: Relaxation-Based Domain Contraction
children.top_down_role: Convex-relaxation information used to contract variable domains.

assumptions_latex: A convex regional relaxation has feasible set \(Q_R\), and every original feasible point in \(R\) has a representative in \(Q_R\).
A valid incumbent cutoff \(c\) is imposed when only points with objective at most \(c\) remain relevant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Coordinate extrema over the cutoff relaxation define certified contracted intervals containing every regionally feasible point capable of meeting the cutoff.

notation.meaning: Relaxation variable representing original coordinate i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization-based bound tightening over a cutoff convex relaxation.

source_refs.locator: 3.12 The GOP in a Branch and Bound Framework p. 114

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a regional relaxation \(Q_R\), relaxation objective \(\ell_R\), and cutoff \(c\), define \(Q_R^c=\{z\in Q_R:\ell_R(z)\leq c\}\). For each represented coordinate \(z_i\), solve \(l_i' = \inf\{z_i:z\in Q_R^c\}\) and \(u_i' = \sup\{z_i:z\in Q_R^c\}\), using certified outward rounding when values are numerical. Replace the current interval by its intersection with \([l_i',u_i']\). If \(Q_R^c=\varnothing\) is certified, fathom \(R\); otherwise iterate selected coordinates until no material contraction occurs or a work limit is reached.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimize each variable over the cutoff convex relaxation to obtain certified tighter bounds; certified emptiness permits regional fathoming.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation-Based Domain Contraction

source_witnesses.locator: 3.12 The GOP in a Branch and Bound Framework p. 114

children.title: Solver Representation Interface
children.top_down_role: Representation classes determining which convex optimization engines can consume a lower model.

children.title: Polyhedral Models
children.top_down_role: Linear and piecewise-linear lower models.

assumptions_latex: Each affine component \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x+b_i\) is a valid lower bound for \(f(x)\) on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maximum \(m(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq p}(a_i^{\mathsf T}x+b_i)\) is a convex polyhedral underestimator and has a linear epigraph representation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite piecewise-affine convex lower models and their linear epigraph formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite polyhedral lower model on \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) has the form \(m(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq p}\{a_i^{\mathsf T}x+b_i\}\), where every component satisfies \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x+b_i\leq f(x)\) for all \(x\in C\). Then \(m\) is convex and \(m(x)\leq f(x)\) on \(C\). Introducing an epigraph variable \(t\), minimizing \(m\) over additional convex constraints is represented by minimizing \(t\) subject to \(t\geq a_i^{\mathsf T}x+b_i\) for \(i=1,\ldots,p\), together with those constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral lower model is the maximum of finitely many valid affine minorants and is represented by one linear epigraph inequality per minorant.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Models

children.title: Smooth Convex Models
children.top_down_role: Differentiable convex lower models for nonlinear convex solvers.

assumptions_latex: The domain \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is open and convex.
The function \(u:C\to\mathbb R\) is continuously differentiable and satisfies \(u(x)\leq f(x)\) on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model is convex exactly when \(u(y)\geq u(x)+\nabla u(x)^{\mathsf T}(y-x)\) for all \(x,y\in C\); its gradient supplies valid affine lower supports.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order characterization of differentiable convex lower models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and convex. A smooth convex lower model of \(f\) is a continuously differentiable function \(u:C\to\mathbb R\) satisfying both \(u(x)\leq f(x)\) for every \(x\in C\) and the first-order convexity condition \(u(y)\geq u(x)+\nabla u(x)^{\mathsf T}(y-x)\) for all \(x,y\in C\). For continuously differentiable \(u\), the latter condition is equivalent to convexity. Consequently, every gradient linearization of \(u\) is an affine underestimator of both \(u\) and \(f\) throughout \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth convex lower model is differentiable, lies below the target, and satisfies the global first-order convexity inequality, making every tangent affine function valid.
knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Convex Models

children.title: Nonsmooth Convex Models
children.top_down_role: Composite and maximum-form models requiring nonsmooth-capable interfaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Convex Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional epigraph and first-order-oracle representations of maximum-form and monotone composite convex models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty open convex set, and let \(h_i:C\to\mathbb{R}\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), be convex. Then \(\phi:C\to\mathbb{R}\), defined by \(\phi(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}h_i(x)\), is convex and has the epigraph representation \[\operatorname{epi}\phi=\{(x,t)\in C\times\mathbb{R}:h_i(x)\le t\text{ for every }i\}.\] For every \(x\in C\), \[\partial\phi(x)=\operatorname{conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{i\in I(x)}\partial h_i(x)\right),\qquad I(x)=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:h_i(x)=\phi(x)\}.\] Thus a first-order interface may return \(\phi(x)\) and an element of \(\partial\phi(x)\). More generally, if \(F_j:C\to\mathbb{R}\), \(j=1,\ldots,p\), are convex and \(g:\mathbb{R}^p\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex and coordinatewise nondecreasing, then \(x\mapsto g(F_1(x),\ldots,F_p(x))\) is convex on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On an open convex domain, a finite maximum of finite convex functions has an exact epigraph representation and an active-function subdifferential formula. A convex coordinatewise-nondecreasing outer function also preserves convexity when composed with convex scalar components.
assumptions_latex: For the composite statement, each \(F_j:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex and \(g:\mathbb{R}^p\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex and coordinatewise nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi\) is convex and is representable by its epigraph constraints or a value-subgradient oracle; the stated monotone composite is also convex.

notation.meaning: Indices attaining the maximum at x.
Convex subdifferential of phi at x.

children.title: Cone-Lift Representation Family
children.top_down_role: Lifted lower models represented through standard convex cones.

children.title: Conic Models
children.top_down_role: Lifted lower models represented through standard nonpolyhedral convex cones.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional lifted conic representation of a convex underestimator's epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^q\) be a closed convex cone, and let \(\phi:C\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be convex. The function \(\phi\) has a \(K\)-conic epigraph lift if there exist an integer \(r\ge0\), matrices \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times n}\) and \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times r}\), and vectors \(b,c\in\mathbb{R}^q\) such that \[\operatorname{epi}\phi=\left\{(x,t)\in C\times\mathbb{R}:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^r,\ Ax+bt+By+c\in K\right\}.\] Consequently, minimizing \(\phi\) over \(C\) is equivalent in optimal value to minimizing \(t\) over the lifted conic set. The projection onto \((x,t)\) must equal the entire epigraph; a mere inclusion does not establish an exact representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic model represents the underestimator epigraph exactly as the projection of an affine conic feasible set.
assumptions_latex: The projected lifted feasible set equals \(\operatorname{epi}\phi\).

children.title: Semidefinite Models
children.top_down_role: Lifted lower models represented through positive-semidefinite matrix constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Semidefinite Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-semidefinite cone lifts for convex underestimators and their epigraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and let \(\phi:C\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be convex. The function \(\phi\) has a semidefinite epigraph lift if there exist integers \(s\ge1\) and \(r\ge0\), real symmetric matrices \(F_0,F_1,\ldots,F_n,G,H_1,\ldots,H_r\in\mathbb{S}^s\), and auxiliary variables \(y\in\mathbb{R}^r\) such that \[\operatorname{epi}\phi=\left\{(x,t)\in C\times\mathbb{R}:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^r,\ F_0+\sum_{i=1}^n x_iF_i+tG+\sum_{j=1}^r y_jH_j\succeq0\right\}.\] Minimizing \(t\) over this lifted set is then exact in optimal value for minimizing \(\phi\) over \(C\). If only inclusion of the lifted projection in \(\operatorname{epi}\phi\) is known, the formulation is a restriction rather than an exact representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A semidefinite model represents the underestimator epigraph exactly as the projection of a linear matrix inequality.
assumptions_latex: All coefficient matrices belong to the same symmetric-matrix space \(\mathbb{S}^s\).
The projection of the linear matrix inequality equals \(\operatorname{epi}\phi\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in C}\phi(x)\) equals the infimum obtained by minimizing \(t\) over the lifted semidefinite feasible set.

notation.meaning: Space of real symmetric matrices of order s.
The symmetric matrix M is positive semidefinite.

children.title: Cone-Lift Selection
children.top_down_role: Representation choices governing lift size, strength, plus solver compatibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Lift Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity-first selection among equivalent cone lifts of the same convex epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose two closed-cone lifts \(L_1\) and \(L_2\) satisfy \(\operatorname{proj}_{x,t}L_1=\operatorname{proj}_{x,t}L_2=\operatorname{epi}\phi\). Exact optimization of \(t\) over either lift therefore yields \(\inf_{x\in C}\phi(x)\). A valid lift-selection rule first requires this projection equality and then may minimize a declared computational criterion, such as cone dimension, number of affine constraints, barrier parameter, sparsity fill, or availability of certified primal-dual residual bounds. A smaller lift is not preferable when it weakens the projection, violates required cone closure, or lacks the numerical certification needed to preserve a rigorous lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose only an exact epigraph lift, then compare cone size, sparsity, solver support, and the availability of rigorous residual certification.
assumptions_latex: Each candidate lift uses a closed convex cone.
Projection equality with the intended epigraph has been established.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: All exact candidate lifts have the same mathematical optimum; selection may therefore use an explicit computational and certification criterion.

notation.meaning: Feasible set of candidate lifted formulation k.
Projection onto original and epigraph variables.

children.title: Numerical Certification Interface
children.top_down_role: Mechanisms preserving rigorous lower bounds across arithmetic and solver boundaries.

children.title: Outward-Rounded Enclosures
children.top_down_role: Certified numerical enclosures for ranges and curvature data.

knowledge_statements.title: Outward-Rounded Enclosures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interval certificates for function ranges, derivatives, and curvature quantities used in convex underestimation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a box \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), an outward-rounded interval evaluation of a real quantity \(q(x)\) is an interval \([\underline q,\overline q]\) whose endpoints are rounded toward \(-\infty\) and \(+\infty\), respectively, and which satisfies \[\{q(x):x\in X\cap\operatorname{dom}q\}\subseteq[\underline q,\overline q].\] For a twice differentiable \(f\), an outward-rounded interval Hessian \(\mathcal H(X)\) must contain every entry of \(\nabla^2f(x)\) for every \(x\in X\). Any rigorously derived \(m\) satisfying \(m\le\lambda_{\min}(H)\) for every \(H\in\mathcal H(X)\) certifies a lower curvature bound on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directed rounding produces intervals guaranteed to contain all exact ranges; an enclosed interval Hessian can certify a valid lower curvature bound.
assumptions_latex: All elementary operations and constants use directed rounding.
\(q\) is defined at every point included in the claimed range.
For curvature certification, \(f\) is twice differentiable on the box.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resulting intervals contain the exact quantities, and \(m\) is a certified lower bound for \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))\) on \(X\).

notation.meaning: Interval enclosure of all Hessians over X.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: containment under directed rounding is the defining invariant of validated interval arithmetic

children.title: Solver-Bound Validation
children.top_down_role: Certification or repair of lower bounds returned by finite-precision convex solvers.

knowledge_statements.title: Solver-Bound Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-feasibility certificate for rigorous lower bounds from finite-precision conic optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the conic problem \[p^*=\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}z:Az=b,\ z\in K\},\] where \(K\) is a closed convex cone. If a computed vector \(y\) is validated, using rigorous arithmetic, to satisfy \(c-A^{\mathsf T}y\in K^*\), then weak duality gives the certified bound \(b^{\mathsf T}y\le p^*\), regardless of primal attainment. An approximate solver objective is not itself a certificate. When exact dual feasibility fails, the returned point must be repaired to a rigorously feasible dual point or its objective must be reduced by a rigorously derived residual-error allowance before being used as a global lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solver lower bound is rigorous only after dual feasibility is validated or residual errors are safely repaired and deducted.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone and \(K^*\) is its dual cone.
All feasibility and objective enclosures used for certification are rigorously rounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A validated dual-feasible \(y\) certifies \(b^{\mathsf T}y\le p^*\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conic weak duality makes any rigorously dual-feasible objective a lower-bound certificate

children.title: Bound-Validity Failures

children.title: Domain-Sign Validity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Use of local formulas outside their certified domain, sign, or singularity regime.

children.title: Domain-Regime Violations
children.top_down_role: Failures caused by applying local underestimators outside their certified domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Regime Violations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by applying an underestimator outside the domain on which its derivation is valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(u(x)\le f(x)\) has been established only for \(x\in D_0\), then using \(u\) on a relaxation domain \(D\) is valid only when \(D\subseteq D_0\cap\operatorname{dom}f\), unless a separate extension theorem is supplied. For example, \(f(x)=-\log x\) is convex on \((0,\infty)\), and its tangent at \(x=1\), namely \(u(x)=1-x\), satisfies \(u(x)\le f(x)\) there. A node or relaxation containing \(x\le0\) lies outside \(\operatorname{dom}f\); the tangent inequality supplies no finite underestimator of the original expression on that enlarged set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An underestimator proved on one domain cannot be used on a larger relaxation that includes points where the function or derivation is invalid.
assumptions_latex: The inequality \(u\le f\) is known only on \(D_0\).
The optimization relaxation is evaluated on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without \(D\subseteq D_0\cap\operatorname{dom}f\), the claimed lower bound is not certified.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the displayed logarithmic tangent example directly exhibits the domain boundary

children.title: Sign-Regime Violations
children.top_down_role: Failures caused by using sign-sensitive constructions under incompatible sign conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Sign-Regime Violations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of an underestimation inequality when a variable crosses the sign regime supporting the curvature argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The reciprocal function \(f(x)=1/x\) satisfies \(f''(x)=2/x^3\), so it is convex on \((0,\infty)\) and concave on \(( -\infty,0)\). Its tangent at \(x=1\) is \(u(x)=2-x\), and convexity certifies \(u(x)\le f(x)\) only for \(x>0\). Extending that tangent across the sign boundary destroys underestimation: at \(x=-1\), \(u(-1)=3\) while \(f(-1)=-1\). Thus a relaxation using this tangent is invalid whenever its domain admits negative values, even if zero itself is excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Curvature can reverse across a sign boundary; the positive-domain tangent to the reciprocal becomes an overestimator at negative points.
assumptions_latex: The tangent underestimator is derived from convexity on \((0,\infty)\).
The relaxed domain admits at least one negative point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inequality \(u(x)\le f(x)\) does not extend from the positive to the negative sign regime.

notation.meaning: Tangent at x equal to one.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the explicit derivative and point evaluation verify the sign-regime failure

children.title: Singularity-Boundary Exposure
children.top_down_role: Validity loss near singularities or transitions between certified regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Singularity-Boundary Exposure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of finite enclosures when a relaxation box reaches a function's singular boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=-\log x\) on \((0,1]\). As \(x\downarrow0\), \(f(x)\to+\infty\), \(f'(x)=-1/x\to-\infty\), and \(f''(x)=1/x^2\to+\infty\). Hence any closed interval \(X=[0,b]\) with \(b>0\) touches a singular boundary and admits no finite enclosure of the range, gradient, or curvature over \(X\cap\operatorname{dom}f\). An underestimator construction requiring finite derivative or Hessian bounds cannot be certified on such a box; the box must be separated from zero or treated by a singularity-aware formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A box touching a singular boundary may have unbounded function, derivative, or curvature ranges, invalidating constructions that require finite enclosures.
assumptions_latex: The relaxation interval contains points arbitrarily close to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No finite range, gradient, or Hessian enclosure exists on \(X\cap\operatorname{dom}f\).

notation.meaning: Relaxation interval exposed to the singular boundary.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the displayed limits directly establish unbounded enclosure quantities

children.title: Uncertified Curvature Information
children.top_down_role: Curvature estimates insufficient to guarantee convexity or underestimation.

knowledge_statements.title: Uncertified Curvature Information
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of convexification when a Hessian lower bound is estimated but not rigorously enclosed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=-x^2\) on \([-1,1]\), the exact curvature is \(f''(x)=-2\). An \(\alpha\)-type underestimator has the form \[u_\alpha(x)=f(x)+\alpha(-1-x)(1-x),\qquad \alpha\ge0.\] Because \((-1-x)(1-x)\le0\) on the interval, \(u_\alpha\le f\); moreover, \(u_\alpha''(x)=-2+2\alpha\), so convexity requires \(\alpha\ge1\). If an uncertified curvature estimate incorrectly asserts the lower bound \(0\), it permits \(\alpha=0\), leaving \(u_0=f\) nonconvex. Thus sampled or floating-point curvature estimates cannot certify a convex underestimator without a rigorous global enclosure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An erroneous curvature estimate can select insufficient convexification; for negative quadratic curvature, zero correction leaves the model nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Convexity requires \(\alpha\ge1\); the uncertified choice \(\alpha=0\) fails.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct differentiation verifies the curvature threshold and failure

children.title: Finite-Precision Invalidity
children.top_down_role: Loss of rigor through rounding, unsafe constants, or solver tolerances.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Precision Invalidity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of lower-bound validity through upward rounding, infeasible dual iterates, or unaccounted solver tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A numerical value \(L\) is a valid lower bound for an optimization problem with optimal value \(p^*\) only if \(L\le p^*\) is established in exact or validated arithmetic. For \[p^*=\min\{x:0\le x\le1\}=0,\] the solver-reported value \(\widehat L=10^{-16}\) is not a lower bound because \(\widehat L>p^*\), however small the discrepancy. Likewise, an approximate dual objective reported without accounting for dual infeasibility, unsafe constants, or rounding error is not a certified lower bound, although it may happen to lie below \(p^*\). Solver tolerances quantify selected numerical residuals; by themselves they do not establish the directed inequality required for a rigorous global lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even a tiny upward error can invalidate a reported lower bound. An approximate value lacking validated error control is uncertified, though it is not necessarily numerically above the true optimum.
assumptions_latex: The exact optimal value is denoted by \(p^*\).
The claimed certificate is a floating-point value \(\widehat L\).
No validated error allowance has been deducted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without validated control establishing \(\widehat L\le p^*\), the claimed lower bound is uncertified and can be invalid even when the numerical error is arbitrarily small.

source_refs.locator: 3.6 Finite epsilon-Convergence and epsilon-Global Optimality p. 87

children.title: Analytic Envelope Pathologies
children.top_down_role: Closure, attainment, and properness difficulties in envelope representations.

children.title: Closure-Sensitive Domain-Epigraph Pathologies
children.top_down_role: Closure-sensitive changes in envelope objects.

children.title: Nonclosed Feasible Domains
children.top_down_role: Envelope behavior associated with excluded boundary points in feasible domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Feasible Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment and closed-epigraph conclusions can fail on convex but nonclosed feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(0,1)\) and \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) be given by \(f(x)=x\). The set \(D\) is convex but not closed, and \[\inf_{x\in D}f(x)=0\] while no \(x\in D\) attains this value. Moreover, the relative epigraph \(\{(x,t):0<x<1,\ t\ge x\}\) is not closed in \(\mathbb{R}^2\); its closure contains \((0,0)\), whose first coordinate is infeasible for the original problem. Consequently, replacing a nonclosed domain or epigraph by its closure can preserve the infimum yet create spurious minimizers and invalidate conclusions that require attainment on the original feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On an open convex domain, the infimum may be unattained, and epigraph closure may introduce boundary minimizers absent from the original problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The infimum equals \(0\) but is unattained, and closure introduces the extraneous boundary point \((0,0)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the explicit open-interval example directly establishes nonattainment and nonclosed epigraph geometry

children.title: Nonclosed Epigraph Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometric pathologies arising when relevant epigraph sets lack closure.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Epigraph Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A convex envelope on a nonclosed domain need not have a closed epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(0,1)\) and \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) satisfy \(f(x)=0\). Its convex envelope relative to \(D\) is \(g=f\). Consequently, \[\operatorname{epi}_D g=\{(x,t)\in D\times\mathbb R:t\geq0\}=(0,1)\times[0,\infty).\] This epigraph is convex but not closed in \(\mathbb R^2\), because \((0,0)\) and \((1,0)\) are excluded limit points. Thus convexity of an underestimator does not imply closed epigraph geometry when its domain is nonclosed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The zero function on an open interval is convex, but its relative epigraph omits boundary limit points and is therefore not closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}_D(\operatorname{conv}_D f)=(0,1)\times[0,\infty)\) is convex and nonclosed.

notation.meaning: greatest convex underestimator of f on D
epigraph of g relative to domain D

children.title: Closure-Induced Envelope Changes
children.top_down_role: Changes in underestimation objects produced by closure operations.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure-Induced Envelope Changes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closing an extended-real formulation may add finite boundary values to its envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(0,1)\), and define \(F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) by \(F(x)=0\) for \(x\in D\) and \(F(x)=+\infty\) otherwise. The greatest convex function dominated by \(F\) equals \(0\) on \(D\) and \(+\infty\) outside \(D\); it is not lower semicontinuous. Its lower-semicontinuous convex closure is \[F^{**}(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\in[0,1],\\+\infty,&x\notin[0,1].\end{cases}\] Hence epigraph closure changes the envelope at both boundary points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closing the epigraph of the zero function on an open interval assigns finite envelope values at the two previously excluded endpoints.
assumptions_latex: Convex closure means the lower-semicontinuous convex envelope in \(\mathbb R\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F^{**}=0\) on \([0,1]\), so closure changes the values at \(0\) and \(1\).

notation.meaning: Fenchel biconjugate, equivalently the lower-semicontinuous convex closure of F

children.title: Unbounded-Domain Pathologies
children.top_down_role: Improper envelopes, absent affine minorants, and recession effects.

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded-Domain Pathologies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: On an unbounded domain, a finite function may have no affine minorant and an improper convex envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be \(f(x)=-x^2\). No affine function \(a(x)=mx+b\) satisfies \(a(x)\leq f(x)\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R\), since \(x^2+mx+b\leq0\) cannot hold for all \(x\). Moreover, every convex \(g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}\) satisfying \(g\leq f\) is identically \(-\infty\). Therefore the extended-real convex envelope of \(f\) on its unbounded domain is improper: \(\operatorname{conv}_{\mathbb R}f\equiv-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The concave quadratic on the whole line admits no affine minorant; allowing improper values, its convex envelope is identically minus infinity.
assumptions_latex: Convex underestimators may take the value \(-\infty\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}_{\mathbb R}f\equiv-\infty\), and no finite affine minorant exists.

notation.meaning: greatest extended-real convex underestimator of f on the real line

children.title: Limit-Representation Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Envelope changes or missing representations caused by discontinuity and nonattainment.

children.title: Envelope Discontinuities
children.top_down_role: Abrupt changes in envelope values or local representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Envelope Discontinuities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary continuity can fail even for a finite convex envelope on a closed interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:[0,1]\to\mathbb R\) by \(f(0)=1\) and \(f(x)=0\) for \(x\in(0,1]\). For every \(x,y\in[0,1]\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), the convexity inequality holds, so \(f\) is convex and is its own convex envelope. Nevertheless, \[\lim_{x\downarrow0}\operatorname{conv}_{[0,1]}f(x)=0<1=\operatorname{conv}_{[0,1]}f(0).\] Thus a finite convex envelope may be discontinuous at a boundary point when lower semicontinuity is not imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex function may jump upward at the endpoint of its domain, so its convex envelope need not be boundary-continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}_{[0,1]}f=f\) and this envelope is discontinuous at \(0\).

notation.meaning: greatest convex underestimator of f on the closed interval

children.title: Underestimator Nonattainment
children.top_down_role: Cases where limiting lower-envelope values lack realizing representatives.

knowledge_statements.title: Underestimator Nonattainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The affine-minorant supremum representing a convex function need not be attained at a boundary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R\) be \(g(x)=-\sqrt{x}\). This function is convex and equals the pointwise supremum of its affine minorants. At \(x=0\), that supremum equals \(g(0)=0\), but no finite affine minorant \(a(x)=mx+b\) attains it. Indeed, attainment would require \(b=0\), while \(mx\leq-\sqrt{x}\) for all \(x>0\) would imply \(m\leq-1/\sqrt{x}\) for every \(x>0\), which no finite \(m\) satisfies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For minus square root, affine minorants approach the boundary value zero, but no finite affine minorant touches the function at zero.
assumptions_latex: Only finite real-valued affine minorants are admitted
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(0)=\sup\{a(0):a\text{ affine},\ a\leq g\}\), but the supremum is not attained.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary boundary-subgradient counterexample verified algebraically

children.title: Representation Loss at Limit Points
children.top_down_role: Missing envelope representations associated with boundary or sequence limits.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation Loss at Limit Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Supporting affine representations at interior points can lose every finite representative at a boundary limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(g(x)=-\sqrt{x}\) on \([0,\infty)\), let \(x_k>0\) with \(x_k\downarrow0\). The tangent minorant at \(x_k\) is \[a_k(x)=-\sqrt{x_k}-\frac{x-x_k}{2\sqrt{x_k}},\] and satisfies \(a_k\leq g\) with \(a_k(x_k)=g(x_k)\). Its slope is \(-1/(2\sqrt{x_k})\to-\infty\); hence \((a_k)\) has no finite-affine coefficient limit representing \(g\) at \(0\). Although \(a_k(0)=-\sqrt{x_k}/2\to g(0)\), support is lost at the limit point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tangents support minus square root at positive points, but their slopes diverge as the points approach zero, leaving no finite limiting support.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a_k(0)\to g(0)\), but no finite affine support is obtained as a coefficient limit of \((a_k)\).

notation.meaning: tangent affine minorant of g at x_k

children.title: Relaxation Weakness-Stagnation Boundary
children.top_down_role: Valid lower models that remain too weak for effective certification.

children.title: Wide-Domain Weakness
children.top_down_role: Large gaps caused by broad variable and expression ranges.

knowledge_statements.title: Wide-Domain Weakness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The absolute gap of a bilinear convex envelope grows quadratically with box width.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(W>0\), consider \(f(x,y)=xy\) on \([0,W]^2\). Its convex envelope is \[g_W(x,y)=\max\{0,\,W(x+y)-W^2\}.\] At the box center, \(g_W(W/2,W/2)=0\), whereas \(f(W/2,W/2)=W^2/4\). Hence the relaxation gap at that point is \(W^2/4\). In particular, broadening the common variable range from width \(W\) to width \(cW\) multiplies this absolute gap by \(c^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bilinear term on a square box, the center gap of the convex envelope is one quarter of the squared box width.

notation.meaning: convex envelope of the bilinear function on the square box

children.title: Dependency-Wrapping Inflation Mechanisms

children.title: Repeated-Variable Dependency Loss
children.top_down_role: Relaxation weakness caused by treating repeated occurrences of a variable independently.

knowledge_statements.title: Repeated-Variable Dependency Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Treating repeated occurrences independently can enlarge an exact singleton range into a nontrivial interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in[0,1]\) and \(f(x)=x-x\). The exact range is \(f([0,1])=\{0\}\). If the two occurrences are replaced by independent variables \(x_1,x_2\in[0,1]\) without the linking constraint \(x_1=x_2\), the lifted expression \(\widehat f(x_1,x_2)=x_1-x_2\) has range \([-1,1]\). Thus occurrence-wise relaxation loses the repeated-variable dependency and creates a strict relaxation gap, even though the original expression is identically zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separating the two appearances of x in x minus x changes its exact range from zero to the interval from minus one to one.
assumptions_latex: The relaxed copies \(x_1,x_2\) are not linked

notation.meaning: occurrence-wise lifted expression with independent variable copies

children.title: Interval Wrapping Inflation
children.top_down_role: Progressive enclosure growth caused by repeated set-based propagation.

knowledge_statements.title: Interval Wrapping Inflation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Repeated interval hull operations can enlarge a set even when the composed exact map is the identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B=[-1,1]^2\), and let \(R\) be rotation through \(\pi/4\). Exact set propagation gives \(R^{-1}(R(B))=B\). Coordinatewise interval propagation first replaces \(R(B)\) by its interval hull \([ -\sqrt2,\sqrt2]^2\). Applying the interval extension of \(R^{-1}\) to that box yields \([-2,2]^2\). Therefore an identity composition can double every coordinate width solely because the intermediate rotated set is wrapped in an axis-aligned interval box.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Boxing a rotated square and then rotating back produces a box twice as wide, although the exact composed transformation is the identity.
assumptions_latex: Intermediate sets are replaced by coordinatewise interval hulls
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R^{-1}(R(B))=B\), while interval propagation returns \([-2,2]^2\).

notation.meaning: rotation of the plane through angle pi/4
smallest axis-aligned interval box containing a set

children.title: Dependency-Preserving Representations
children.top_down_role: Representations that retain selected variable relationships to limit relaxation inflation.

knowledge_statements.title: Dependency-Preserving Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shared lifts preserve repeated-variable identities that independent occurrence-wise lifts destroy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an expression contain several occurrences of a variable \(x\in D\). A dependency-preserving lift introduces one shared variable \(z\) and the linking equation \(z=x\), then substitutes that same \(z\) at every occurrence. For the expression \(f(x)=x-x\), the lifted feasible set is \[L=\{(x,z,t):x\in[0,1],\ z=x,\ t=z-z\}.\] Its projection onto \((x,t)\) is exactly \(\{(x,0):x\in[0,1]\}\); consequently, the representation preserves the original graph and range.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Using one linked auxiliary variable for every repeated occurrence preserves the original graph; for x minus x, the represented value remains exactly zero.
assumptions_latex: Every occurrence is replaced by the same linked variable \(z\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_{x,t}L=\{(x,f(x)):x\in[0,1]\}\).

notation.meaning: projection onto the original variable and expression-value coordinates

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exactness follows directly from the linking equation and projection
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The shared linked lift projects exactly to the original graph, and representation is the correct content kind for this leaf. No authoritative source with a specific locator is supplied, so the record remains needs_source.

children.title: Composition-Gap Accumulation
children.top_down_role: Progressive loss of strength through recursive propagation.

knowledge_statements.title: Composition-Gap Accumulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform underestimation errors propagate additively and are amplified by downstream Lipschitz constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h_i=\phi_i\circ h_{i-1}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), with \(h_0(x)=x\). Suppose each \(\phi_i\) is nondecreasing and \(L_i\)-Lipschitz on the relevant range, and an underestimator \(\underline\phi_i\) satisfies \(0\leq\phi_i(t)-\underline\phi_i(t)\leq\delta_i\). Define \(\underline h_0=h_0\) and \(\underline h_i=\underline\phi_i\circ\underline h_{i-1}\). Then \[0\leq h_m(x)-\underline h_m(x)\leq\sum_{i=1}^{m}\delta_i\prod_{j=i+1}^{m}L_j.\] Thus local composition gaps accumulate and may be amplified through recursive propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a monotone Lipschitz composition chain, every local underestimation error contributes to the final gap after amplification by later Lipschitz constants.
assumptions_latex: Each \(\phi_i\) is nondecreasing and \(L_i\)-Lipschitz on all encountered values
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\leq h_m-\underline h_m\leq\sum_{i=1}^{m}\delta_i\prod_{j=i+1}^{m}L_j\) pointwise.

notation.meaning: recursively propagated underestimator through stage i
stage-i Lipschitz constant and uniform local underestimation error

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard recursive Lipschitz error-propagation inequality
